text: Chicago's Black population grew from about 40,000 in 1910 to roughly 234,000 by 1930, and about 278,000 by 1940.
Nearly seven times as many people in thirty years.
They needed somewhere to live, and the city had decided in advance where that would be.
Most newcomers were funneled into a narrow strip on the South Side that people called the Black Belt.
It ran for miles north to south but was only a few blocks wide.
Inside it, demand far outran supply, and landlords took full advantage.
They chopped single apartments into tiny units called kitchenettes, sometimes a hundred square feet, with one bathroom and one stove shared down a hall.
Six or seven families might crowd into a flat once leased to two.
A Chicago Housing Authority study in the late 1930s found that nearly half of kitchenette tenants, about 45 percent, were paying more than 30 percent of their income just for rent.
Clair Drake and Horace Cayton, who mapped this world in their 1945 study Black Metropolis, described the same blocks holding several times the people they were built for.
So Black families paid more, for less, and the color line was the reason.
It left them nowhere else to go.
